meta.title: Seoul Tore Down a Downtown Highway | What Happened to the Traffic, and to the Stream Underneath
meta.family_reason: The script answers 'what happened': one event (a city demolishes its own elevated highway), then a rewind, then the aftermath. B's beat order (peak first, rewind, same scene again, aftermath, closing declaration, a 'not yet' fact) fits. Caveat: B's selection rule assumes original on-site footage that is itself the spectacle; this brief allows no news archive, so the peak is carried by a cross-section diagram plus generic stock that is never labeled as the real event.
meta.logline: Seoul removed a highway that carried over 100,000 vehicles a day to uncover a buried stream; the feared traffic disaster was milder than expected, the stream brought measurable gains, and it still has to be pumped full every day.
meta.audience_belief: Remove a highway from the middle of a city and the traffic gets worse.
meta.axis_fact: Twelve lanes of road (4 elevated + 8 at street level) were cut to four, on a corridor used by about 168,000 vehicles a day (Seoul Metropolitan Government, June 2003).
meta.materials: Open-license live-action stock (Pexels, Pixabay, Mixkit, Coverr): Cheonggyecheon today, Seoul streets and traffic, generic elevated highway and demolition, people by water at night. Vector graphics: simple map, before/after cross-section, numbers, typography. No commissioned shooting, no generated images, no news archive footage.

sources.label: Seoul Metropolitan Government, 'Cheonggyecheon' (official English page), viewed 2026-11
sources.checked: Restoration period July 2003 to September 2005 (two years, three months); restored length 5.84 km; cost KRW 386.739 billion (as of 2005); covering project began after the 1950s.

sources.label: Landscape Performance Series (Landscape Architecture Foundation), 'Cheonggyecheon Stream Restoration Project' case study brief
sources.checked: 3.6 miles (5.84 km); temperatures along the stream 3.3 to 5.9 C cooler than on a parallel road 4-7 blocks away; fish species 4 to 25 between 2003 and end of 2008; 'contributed to' a 15.1% increase in bus ridership and 3.3% in subway ridership in Seoul between 2003 and end of 2008; average 64,000 visitors daily; budget about $380 million. Note: the brief's '639%' is the ratio of all counted species after/before (626/98), not a rise 'from 62 to 864'; 62 to 308 is plants only.

sources.label: Seoul Metropolitan Government newsroom (내 손안에 서울), '청계천 주변교통 걱정되시죠?', 2003-06-26
sources.checked: Daily traffic 168,000 vehicles = Cheonggye elevated highway 102,000 (4 lanes, both directions) + Cheonggyecheon-ro 66,000 (8 lanes); works start July 1, 2003; the elevated highway is removed and only 4 of the 8 street lanes remain; the press was warning of '교통대란' (traffic chaos/disaster); the city's worst-case simulation had downtown speed falling from 21.0 to 18.3 km/h.

sources.label: Seoul Solution (Seoul Metropolitan Government policy archive), 'Removal of Overpasses in Seoul to Improve the Cityscape & Transportation Environment', 2015
sources.checked: 'The removal of this first overpass resulted in a better cityscape and traffic congestion was not as severe as had been expected'; 'some worried about severe congestion ... but the current condition near the stream is not severe'; Table 1 lists 13 overpasses removed after the Cheonggye Overpass, through July 2014. The same page lists the overpass as built in 1969 and calls it a '5 km stretch' (differs from other sources, see S8).

sources.label: The Guardian, 'Everyone thought it would cause gridlock: the highway that Seoul turned into a stream', 2025-01-17
sources.checked: Quote of local resident Park Byung-chul: 'Initially, everyone thought it would cause gridlock. But people adapted. Now we can't imagine the highway ever being here.'; start ceremony July 1, 2003; Lee Myung-bak won the 2002 mayoral election campaigning to restore the stream; completed in 27 months at 386bn won; needs more than 48,000 tonnes of water pumped daily (40,000 treated Han River water + 8,300 groundwater), costing 2.9bn won a year; original stream was seasonal; Seoul has since removed 16 other elevated highways; Seoul Institute: 3.6 C cooler than nearby streets; 666 species in a 2022 survey; more than 12 million visitors a year. The article says the elevated highway carried '168,000 cars daily'; S3 shows that figure includes the street beneath. The reporter's byline was not captured when the page was read; confirm it before crediting on screen.

sources.label: Hong Kal, 'Flowing Back to the Future: The Cheonggye Stream Restoration and the Remaking of Seoul', The Asia-Pacific Journal: Japan Focus, 2011
sources.checked: Via search-result excerpt only: 'In spite of fierce resistance especially from sidewalk vendors, the city government successfully cleared the area by force'; opposition came from 'poor residents, merchants, and especially "illegal" sidewalk vendors in the area, who were to be evicted to clear space'; 5.8-kilometer-long expressway overpass; water pumped from the Han River.

sources.label: Sustainability 8(11):1178 (MDPI), 'How Do Mega Projects Alter the City to Be More Sustainable? Spatial Changes Following the Seoul Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project in South Korea', 2016
sources.checked: Via search-result excerpt only: 60,000 shops, 220,000 merchants and over 3,000 street vendors along the corridor; 1,045 merchants relocated to the Garden Five mall (opened 2010), of whom about 100 remained; the relocation 'turned out to be a failure'. Meeting counts differ between sources (42,000 here, about 4,200 elsewhere) and are not used.

sources.label: Disagreements not resolved on screen (New York Times 2009-07-16; ITDP 2003-05-01; USACE/Seoul slides; KSCE Journal of Civil Engineering 2015)
sources.checked: Via search-result excerpts only. Korea Herald (2015-10-01) and Seoul slides hosted by USACE: opened Oct. 1, 2005. NYT: nearly all the water on a typical day is pumped from the Han River through seven miles of pipe; fish species 4 to 25. ITDP: 120,000 cars used the corridor daily. Seoul slides: highway built 1968-1976, stream covered 1958-1978, 170,000 vehicles/day. KSCE 2015 cost-benefit paper: congestion costs had been underestimated before the project and the benefit-cost ratio at completion was 0.75. These are the reason the script says 'over 100,000', 'decades earlier', 'milder than feared' and 'over 40,000 tons'.

cast.look: Flat vector cross-section looking along the road: gray elevated deck on a row of concrete piers, a street-level road beneath it, and under that street a dark box culvert. Buildings as plain dark blocks left and right. After state: no deck, an open channel with a thin band of water in the middle, two lanes on each bank.
cast.fixed: The drawing sits in the lower third and the outer thirds of the frame; the middle band stays empty and dark for the text. Lane marks are countable: 4 on the deck, 8 on the street before; 2 + 2 after. Never drawn with a place name on it.

cast.look: Simple dark vector map of Seoul: the Han River as one wide curve, one short east-west line north of it in the old center.
cast.fixed: Only one geographic label, 'Han River'. The line is amber while it is a road and turns blue once it is the stream.

cast.look: Live-action stock of the real Cheonggyecheon: shallow water between stone walls about one story below street level, stepping stones, office towers above.
cast.fixed: Must be the real location. Darken and keep the brightest part of the picture out of the center band.

review_notes: Manual check, overlap: c02 names the action the picture shows ('tearing down'). Kept because family B's hook is defined as the action written in the present tense; the text adds what the picture cannot ('a city', 'its own').

Manual check, last line: c19 gives a new figure, which the general ending rule (no new information) forbids but family B's last card ('a fact that is not yet solved') requires. The callback 'every day' appears only in c03 and c19.
Manual check, axis fact: the lane count sits at 0:21-0:26 (about 27%), earlier than 'the middle', because in family B the context comes in the rewind and everything after it is aftermath.

Manual check, naming: family B asks for anonymous, then category, then real name. The category step is skipped ('a city' goes straight to 'Seoul, South Korea' on the date card) to stay inside 90 seconds.

Manual check, scope: the script closes on two unsolved points (vendors cleared out, pumped water) and does not sum the project up as a success. Left out for length: project cost, the Garden Five merchant relocation, the 2015 cost-benefit paper's 0.75 ratio, visitor counts.
Stand-in footage: c01, c02, c08, c10, c12 and c16 are generic stock and carry no place or date label. Every shot that is presented as the stream (c09, c14, c17, c18, c19) must be the real location.

Editor pass after skill 0.6.0: c02 no longer shows the demolition with generic excavator footage. A stand-in clip must not show the event itself (04, section 8), so the peak is carried by the cross-section from the first text card.

Editor pass: c08 "the press warned of a traffic disaster" was changed to "many feared severe congestion", which is what the sources support (S4: "some worried about severe congestion"; S5: "everyone thought it would cause gridlock").
Editor pass: eight cards were lengthened to meet the English reading floor (words/3 + 2 s). Family B runs fast by design, but the floor is a production limit, not a style choice. Total is now 90 s.
Editor pass: c12 became a diagram so that the 2003-2008 label does not sit on stand-in bus footage. c10 and c16 keep source labels without a year.
Still open before production: c16 (vendors cleared out) rests on two sources that were read only as search excerpts. A person should open Kal (2011) before this card is used.
assumptions: Length set to 85 seconds inside the 75-90 second brief.
Text is in US English; on-screen distance is in miles with kilometers in the corner label; temperature stays in Celsius as in the sources, with a Fahrenheit equivalent in the corner label.
No title card (family B does not require one).
Actual-location stock footage of the stream is typed 실사; generic stand-in footage is typed 스톡 and must not carry a place or date label.
Project cost (KRW 386.7 billion official; dollar conversions range from $281 million to about $380 million) is left off screen because one more number did not fit the length.

beats.name: 정점 먼저
beats.job: Show the act itself in the present tense with an unnamed subject: a city is demolishing a working highway.
beats.scene: What an elevated highway through a downtown looks like, what demolition of concrete looks like, and that there are two levels of road with something dark under them.
beats.text: That the city is doing this to itself, and how many vehicles the highway carries every day.

beats.name: 되감기
beats.job: Rewind: date, place, and what was put under the road decades earlier.
beats.scene: Where in the city the line runs (map) and where the water sits relative to the road (cross-section).
beats.text: Date, city name, who buried it and when.

beats.name: 같은 장면 다시
beats.job: Look at the same cross-section again knowing what is underneath: the plan and the warning.
beats.scene: Where the twelve lanes are and what replaces them; what a jammed street looks like.
beats.text: The purpose (to uncover it), the lane count, who warned and of what.

beats.name: 후속
beats.job: Aftermath in the past tense, in one block: opening, the jam that was milder than feared, a resident's words, bus ridership, temperature, fish.
beats.scene: The stream as it looks now, moving traffic and buses, where the temperature was compared, life in the water.
beats.text: Elapsed time, the comparison with the fear, the quote, percentages and counts with their years.

beats.name: 종결 선언
beats.job: How the event ended for the city: it kept removing overpasses.
beats.scene: A row of overpass icons disappearing one by one.
beats.text: The count and who did it.

beats.name: 마지막 카드
beats.job: What is still not solved, stated as fact: the vendors who were cleared out, and water that has to be pumped every day.
beats.scene: A street market, water coming out of a built wall, people walking beside the stream at night.
beats.text: Who was cleared out, that the water does not arrive by itself, the daily tonnage.
